transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it’s nice to meet you too. Thanks for fitting me in. I, uh... well, I guess I’m here because things have just gotten to a point where I can't really ignore them anymore. I'm a software developer, and I've always juggled a lot of different projects, which used to feel fine, or at least manageable. I mean, I made it through grad school, I've been in the industry for a long time, so you'd think I'd have a solid system down by now at my age. But what finally pushed me to actually pick up the phone and come in today is that I just... I can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. 

It’s like everything is happening all at once and I have absolutely no filter or sorting mechanism for it. Just to give you an idea, right now at work, I’ve got these really dense patent notes I need to finalize for a new architecture we're submitting, and at the exact same time, I’m supposed to be doing all this prep for a technical workshop I’m leading. And then outside of my main job, I do some digital art, and I have these gallery deadlines coming up that I completely underestimated when I agreed to them. Plus, there are just the constant, everyday team decisions where my junior devs are waiting on me for direction so they can actually do their jobs. 

It’s just so many pieces, and instead of sitting down and figuring out a rational timeline or a proper schedule, I just... I end up starting whatever is loudest. You know? Like, whatever email just chimed, or whoever just pinged me on Slack, or whatever minor crisis is right in front of my face—that’s what gets my attention, instead of what actually matters or what strategically needs to happen first. I just feel like I'm constantly putting out the nearest fire instead of actually managing my time, and it's completely exhausting. I just can't keep operating like this.
Did you have trouble with attention or staying organized when you were a child?

Yeah, you know, it’s funny you ask that because for the longest time, I didn't really think so. I mean, I made it through grad school, right? So I always just assumed I was fine back then, that I was just a normal kid. But lately, since things have gotten so overwhelming at work, I’ve actually been looking back and thinking about it, and... yeah. It was absolutely there, long before I was even a teenager. 

My mom actually kept all my old report cards from grade school in this big plastic storage bin, and if you look at them, every single year, almost like clockwork, the teachers would write the exact same thing in the comments section. They’d say I was a bright kid, very capable, but that I spent half the day daydreaming. I was always just staring out the window or getting completely lost in my own head instead of paying attention to whatever the lesson was. 

And the organization... oh man, it was a total disaster. I would actually do the homework, which is the crazy part. I’d sit at the kitchen table, do all the math problems, finish the whole worksheet, put my pencil down, and then I would just completely forget to turn it in the next day. It would just sit crumpled up in my desk. Or worse, I’d lose the entire homework folder. I remember having these specific, brightly colored folders that we were supposed to use, and they would just vanish into the abyss of my locker or the bottom of my backpack, and my parents were constantly having to replace them. So, yeah, it wasn't just a college or an adult thing, it was definitely happening way back in elementary school. It's just so frustrating to think about how much extra effort I had to put in just to keep track of a simple piece of paper, you know? Like, why couldn't I just put it in the tray like everyone else did? It just feels like I've been fighting this exact same battle with my brain for forty years.
Have you ever had a period where your mood was unusually high or irritable for several days in a row?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I definitely get stressed, obviously, and when I'm stressed I can get a little snippy, maybe, but not... not like what you're saying, where it's just this constant, unusually high mood or some kind of intense irritability that lasts for days on end. That doesn't really sound like me. 

If anything, my mood is pretty tied to whatever is going wrong with my schedule at that exact moment. Like, if I'm trying to figure out those patent notes I mentioned, and my brain just feels like it's wading through wet concrete, I get frustrated with myself. I'll sit there and think, "Come on, you know this stuff, just focus," and when I can't, yeah, I get annoyed. And maybe if someone interrupts me right then, I might sigh a little too loudly or give a short answer, but it's not a mood that takes over my whole life for days. It's just a reaction to the immediate frustration of not being able to make my brain do what I want it to do. 

And as for feeling unusually high or energetic... no, definitely not. Honestly, I'm usually just tired. Mental fatigue is kind of my baseline these days because I'm spending so much energy just trying to keep all the plates spinning. I don't really have these bursts of feeling on top of the world or having boundless energy. It's more of a constant, low-level exhaustion from trying to manage the chaos. So, no, I haven't really experienced anything like that. Just the regular, everyday frustration of feeling like I'm always two steps behind where I should be.
Did these problems get noticeably worse after a particular stressful event or major change in your life?

Well, yeah, actually. It’s not like it happened overnight, but there was definitely a turning point. So, about a year and a month ago—give or take a few weeks, but right around then—I won this industry award for a piece of software architecture I designed. Which, you know, was great. I was incredibly honored, and it felt like a real validation of all the hard work I’d put in over the years. But the thing about getting recognized like that is it completely shifts how people see you at the company, and suddenly, they want you doing different things. 

So, right after the award, management decided to promote me, or at least shift my role, into something way more coordination-heavy. Instead of just putting my head down and coding—which I’m good at, I can just hyper-focus on the screen and make things work—they wanted me leading multiple teams, setting the strategic vision, running these cross-departmental workshops, and basically being the point person for all these different moving parts. 

And that’s when the wheels completely fell off. I mean, the inattentive stuff, the daydreaming, the losing track of things—that was always there, like I said about my report cards. But I had managed to build a career where I could mostly hide it, or at least compensate for it by just being really good at the technical side. But this new role... it’s all the things I’m terrible at, dialed up to eleven. It’s constant context switching. I’ll be trying to review a junior dev’s code, and then I have to jump into a meeting about budget allocation, and then I have to go back to writing those patent notes, and my brain just... it just blue-screens. It’s been about thirteen months of this now, and it’s just gotten progressively worse because the demands keep piling up and my old coping mechanisms just absolutely do not work for this level of coordination. So, yeah, the award was great for my resume, but it basically threw me into the deep end of exactly the kind of work I’m least equipped to handle, and that’s really when this all became completely unmanageable.
Do you spend a lot of your day worrying excessively about different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I sit around and just... worry about things that aren't happening. It's not like I'm lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling, agonizing over whether the house is going to catch fire or if I'm going to get some terrible disease, or, you know, worrying about the economy or something abstract like that. That's never really been my thing. 

If I'm stressed, it's almost always tied directly to something very tangible and immediate that I'm dropping the ball on. Like, I'll stress about the fact that I have three unread emails from the VP of Engineering that I know I need to respond to, but I can't bring myself to open them because I know I haven't finished the project timeline she asked for on Tuesday. And then I'll stress about the timeline because I can't find the notes I took during the kickoff meeting, which I'm pretty sure I wrote on a legal pad that is now buried somewhere under a mountain of coffee cups and printouts on my desk. So, it's a very specific, practical kind of stress. It's the stress of knowing I'm behind, knowing I'm forgetting things, and knowing that people are waiting on me. 

But it's not this free-floating anxiety, if that makes sense? It's not like my brain is just looking for things to be afraid of. It's more like my brain is acutely aware that it's failing to manage the actual, real-world tasks in front of it, and the stress is just the natural byproduct of that failure. If I actually managed to get my inbox to zero and finish all my reports—which, let's be honest, is a complete fantasy at this point—but if I did, I don't think I'd be worrying about anything at all. I'd probably just take a nap. So, no, I don't think I have that kind of excessive, unprompted worrying you're talking about. It's really just the immediate chaos that gets to me.
